## What does this package do for me?

You have a protein structure and a list of its active-site residues. `msamodel`
implements the Mutation-Stability-Activity (MSA) model of neutral structural
evolution: it predicts how much each part of the structure **diverges** under
neutral evolution, fits that prediction to an observed divergence profile, and
tells you how stability and activity selection shape the result.

The model has two selection parameters: `a1` (selection on **stability**) and `a2`
(selection on **activity**, proximity to the active site). The same predicted
divergence can be read along **two axes** — per residue and per normal mode — and
this overview shows both, end to end.

|                              | what it is                                              |
|------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| **You provide**              | a PDB file; a vector of active-site residue numbers; (to fit) an observed divergence table `{pdb_site, lrmsd_i_obs}` |
| **`msamodel` computes**      | the elastic network model (`setup_enm`), the mutation scan (`generate_spm_data`), the divergence profiles (`calculate_*`), and the fit (`fit_*`) |

## From your structure to a mutation scan

Everything starts from your two inputs. We use the worked example `1znb_A` (zinc
beta-lactamase) that ships with the package; swap in your own file and residues at
the two marked lines:


```r
pdb_file        <- system.file("extdata", "1znb_A.pdb", package = "msamodel")  # <- your PDB path
pdb_site_active <- c(99, 101, 103, 162, 181, 184, 193, 223)                    # <- your active-site residues
```

`msamodel` reads the structure, builds an elastic network model (`wt`), and runs a
single-point-mutation scan (`spm`):


```r
pdb <- bio3d::read.pdb(pdb_file)
wt  <- setup_enm(pdb, node = "ca", model = "ming_wall", d_max = 10.5, frustrated = FALSE)
spm <- generate_spm_data(wt, n_mutations = 10, model = "lfenm", sigma = 0.3,
                         min_sd = 2, pdb_site_active = pdb_site_active, seed = 1024)
#> Processing site 10 of 228 
#> Processing site 20 of 228 
#> Processing site 30 of 228 
#> Processing site 40 of 228 
#> Processing site 50 of 228 
#> Processing site 60 of 228 
#> Processing site 70 of 228 
#> Processing site 80 of 228 
#> Processing site 90 of 228 
#> Processing site 100 of 228 
#> Processing site 110 of 228 
#> Processing site 120 of 228 
#> Processing site 130 of 228 
#> Processing site 140 of 228 
#> Processing site 150 of 228 
#> Processing site 160 of 228 
#> Processing site 170 of 228 
#> Processing site 180 of 228 
#> Processing site 190 of 228 
#> Processing site 200 of 228 
#> Processing site 210 of 228 
#> Processing site 220 of 228
```

(`wt` and `spm` here are identical to the `znb_wt` / `znb_spm` datasets shipped with
the package; if you only want to skim, `data("znb_spm")` loads the prebuilt scan
instead of running the line above.) From the scan we precompute once, for each axis:


```r
pp      <- preprocess_spm(spm)        # per-residue (site) axis
pp_mode <- preprocess_spm_mode(spm)   # per-mode axis
```

## Fit the model, then read divergence two ways

To fit, you supply an **observed** per-residue divergence profile — this is **your**
data, not something `msamodel` computes. The observed divergence (`lrmsd_i_obs`)
comes from comparing homologous structures over an alignment, which is out of scope
for `msamodel`; you bring it as a table with columns `pdb_site` and `lrmsd_i_obs`.
The package ships one for the worked example, `znb_profile`:


```r
data("znb_profile")   # the example observed data; supply your own in this shape
head(znb_profile)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   pdb_site lrmsd_i_obs
#>      <int>       <dbl>
#> 1       20        1.65
#> 2       21        1.68
#> 3       22        1.23
#> 4       23        1.30
#> 5       24        1.95
#> 6       25        1.69
```

We fit the two selection parameters to that observed profile by maximum likelihood:


```r
ml <- fit_lrmsd_i_msa_ml(pp, znb_profile)
c(a1 = ml$a1, a2 = ml$a2)
#>         a1         a2 
#>  0.4580022 42.3021911
```

At that fitted `(a1, a2)`, the model predicts a divergence profile along **each**
axis. The per-residue prediction has an observed counterpart to check against; the
per-mode prediction reads the *same* selection in the normal-mode basis.


```r
# Per-residue: fitted profile vs the observed data
site <- calculate_lrmsd_i_nested_models(pp, ml$a1, ml$a2) |>
  transmute(pdb_site, lrmsd_fit = lrmsd_i_msa) |>
  inner_join(znb_profile, by = "pdb_site") |>
  mutate(nlrmsd_obs = lrmsd_i_obs - mean(lrmsd_i_obs),
         nlrmsd_fit = lrmsd_fit   - mean(lrmsd_fit))

# Per-mode: predicted divergence at the same fitted (a1, a2)
mode <- calculate_dr2_n_msa(pp_mode, ml$a1, ml$a2) |>
  mutate(lrmsd_n = log(sqrt(dr2_n)))
```

**Per residue** — the fitted profile (red) tracks the observed one (grey) along the
chain; this is the model fit to real data. Both are the mean-centered log-RMSD
(`nlrmsd`): the fit constrains the divergence *shape*, not its overall level, so we
compare shapes.

![plot of chunk panel-site](msamodel_files/figure-html/panel-site-1.png)

**Per normal mode** — the *same* fitted model, predicted in the normal-mode basis:
the per-mode log-RMSD (`lrmsd_n`) is largest for the softest (lowest-index) modes,
so a handful of collective motions carry most of the predicted divergence. (This is
a point prediction; no observed mode profile exists to fit against yet.)

![plot of chunk panel-mode](msamodel_files/figure-html/panel-mode-1.png)

Same evolutionary divergence, read per residue and per mode.

## Where to next

- **[Site analysis](site-analysis.html)** — the per-residue arc in full: predict,
  decompose into mutation / stability / activity contributions, sweep `a1`/`a2`,
  fit, and decompose the fitted profile.
- **[Mode analysis](mode-analysis.html)** — the same arc per normal mode.
- **Inference methods** — maximum likelihood is the standard fit shown here;
  `msamodel` also offers a deterministic-posterior fit (adaptive Gauss–Hermite
  quadrature; see `?fit_lrmsd_i_msa_agq`).
